::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" .lexicon-source}
Entry **#109** in Andrew Gelman's [Handy Statistical Lexicon](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2009/05/24/handy_statistic/). Original discussion: [50 shades of gray goes pie-chart](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2014/11/21/50-shades-gray-goes-pie-chart/).
:::

## What it is

The Stroop test shows colour words ("RED," "BLUE") printed in ink of a *different* colour and asks people to name the ink. The mismatch slows them down. That interference is the whole point of the test. Print it in black and white and every word is in black ink. There is no conflict, no interference and no test. A display that removes the one feature it depends on is, in Gelman's joke, the worst visual display of all time.

## Why it matters

The joke points at a common failure in graphics: a display whose key information is carried by a feature that doesn't survive production, viewing or the reader. Examples are colour-coded lines printed in grayscale, legends that depend on colour distinctions colour-blind readers can't see, and charts whose message is in an interaction the layout hides. Ask what channel is carrying the information, and whether that channel survives.

## How it works

Model reaction time (RT) to name the ink colour:

- **Congruent** (word and ink match): baseline RT.
- **Incongruent** (word and ink differ): baseline plus an interference cost, typically on the order of 100 milliseconds or more.
- **Black and white:** the ink is always black, so there is no conflict to measure, and the measured "effect" collapses to zero.

The simulation uses a made-up but realistic set of RT distributions to show the effect disappearing.

## Simulated example

A miniature Stroop display, and simulated reaction times for the colour and grayscale versions.

```{ojs}
import {rng, range, mean, fmt} from "../js/stats.js"
```

```{ojs}
viewof bw = Inputs.toggle({label: "Print in black and white", value: false})
viewof seed = Inputs.range([1, 500], {value: 109, step: 1, label: "Random seed"})
```

```{ojs}
{
  const words = [["RED", "#2166ac"], ["GREEN", "#d6604d"], ["BLUE", "#1a9850"], ["YELLOW", "#984ea3"], ["PURPLE", "#e6ab02"], ["BLUE", "#d6604d"]];
  return html`<div style="font-size: 1.8rem; font-weight: 700; letter-spacing: 0.05em; display:flex; gap:1rem; flex-wrap:wrap; margin: 0.5rem 0 1rem;">
    ${words.map(([w, c]) => html`<span style="color:${bw ? "currentColor" : c}">${w}</span>`)}
  </div>`;
}
```

```{ojs}
stroop = {
  const r = rng(seed);
  const trial = cond => {
    const base = r.lognormal(Math.log(600), 0.15);
    const interference = !bw && cond === "Incongruent" ? r.normal(120, 40) : 0;
    return {cond, rt: base + interference};
  };
  return [...range(400).map(() => trial("Congruent")), ...range(400).map(() => trial("Incongruent"))];
}
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 260,
  x: {label: "Reaction time (ms)", domain: [300, 1200]},
  y: {label: "Trials"},
  color: {legend: true, range: ["#2166ac", "#d6604d"]},
  marks: [Plot.rectY(stroop, Plot.binX({y: "count"}, {x: "rt", fill: "cond", fillOpacity: 0.55, thresholds: 50, mixBlendMode: "multiply"})), Plot.ruleY([0])]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const m = c => mean(stroop.filter(d => d.cond === c).map(d => d.rt));
  return html`<div class="sim-readout">${md`Interference effect (incongruent minus congruent): **${fmt(m("Incongruent") - m("Congruent"), 0)} ms**. ${bw ? "In black and white there is no conflict between word and ink, so the effect vanishes and the display can't do its one job." : "Toggle black and white and watch the effect disappear."}`}</div>`;
}
```

## Key takeaways

::: takeaways
- Know which visual channel carries your display's information.
- Make sure that channel survives printing, projection and colour-blind readers.
- If the message depends on colour, back it up with labels, position or line style.
:::
